entries.speaker: the-stone-roses
entries.found: So I played him The Clash and he went and bought it the next day, and played it every day for about 18 months, before and after school. That got him obsessed with guitar and made him want to play.
entries.citation: Ian Brown, in the Observer's Soundtrack of My Life (2010): of The Clash's first album, which he played John Squire: "he went and bought it the next day, and played it every day for about 18 months, before and after school. That got him obsessed with guitar and made him want to play."
entries.note: Brown says the album "started the Roses in a way"; the obsession described is Squire's, so it is the band's origin, not Brown's own listening.

entries.speaker: the-stone-roses
entries.found: We couldn't wait for the LP and when it came out it blew us away. I still think it's the best UK album ever made.
entries.citation: Ian Brown, in the Observer's Soundtrack of My Life (2010): on the Sex Pistols at 14: "We couldn't wait for the LP and when it came out it blew us away. I still think it's the best UK album ever made."
entries.note: Formative fandom at about 14, before the band; Brown says the whole run of singles was bought on release day.

entries.speaker: st-vincent
entries.note: Only touring with him ("an apprenticeship"); collaboration, not influence.

entries.speaker: joy-division
entries.found: I didn't start thinking about being in a band until I saw the Sex Pistols, and only became a bass player by default, because Bernard [Sumner] had a guitar.
entries.citation: Peter Hook, in the Observer's Soundtrack of My Life (2013): "I didn't start thinking about being in a band until I saw the Sex Pistols, and only became a bass player by default, because Bernard [Sumner] had a guitar."

entries.speaker: joy-division
entries.found: Kraftwerk did a bit, partly because we used to play Trans-Europe Express before Joy Division gigs ... people say they come across as quite Germanic, quite cold, but I always found tracks like Computer Love very romantic.
entries.citation: Peter Hook, in the Observer's Soundtrack of My Life (2013): on Kraftwerk: "we used to play Trans-Europe Express before Joy Division gigs ... people say they come across as quite Germanic, quite cold, but I always found tracks like Computer Love very romantic."
entries.note: Borderline: the quote is mostly about Kraftwerk helping after Ian Curtis died (New Order era); the Joy Division part is playing Trans-Europe Express before gigs.

entries.speaker: joy-division
entries.found: When I came back to Manchester, their first LP [1973's The Human Menagerie ] led me to Roxy, which led me into Bowie.
entries.citation: Peter Hook, in the Observer's Soundtrack of My Life (2013): on hearing Cockney Rebel at 17: "their first LP [1973's The Human Menagerie] led me to Roxy, which led me into Bowie. To that serious side of music beyond crap pop like Mud, Gary Glitter and Racey."
entries.note: Teenage listening before Joy Division, as the way into serious music; thin on Bowie specifically.

entries.speaker: joy-division
entries.note: Old Ways (1985), a New Order-era favourite; Hook says Bernard got him into it.

entries.speaker: the-smiths
entries.found: I already had a certain facility and knew what I wanted to do. But someone gave me this album – and this is after punk, so it was quite a broad-minded thing to do in those days – with the tagline, "There you go, hotshot, with your Johnny Thunders shit – let's see if you can get your head round that." And I must confess it was one of the few times I actually sat down and thought, "Wow, I'm either gonna have to work this out, or give up."
entries.citation: Johnny Marr, in the Observer's Soundtrack of My Life (2013): on Bert Jansch's LA Turnaround: "it was one of the few times I actually sat down and thought, 'Wow, I'm either gonna have to work this out, or give up.'"
entries.note: Already had facility; the album improved his guitar playing, said to be after punk and before the Smiths.

entries.speaker: the-smiths
entries.note: Named with Sparks and Roxy Music as glam records he and Morrissey both liked; not tied to Marr's own music.

entries.speaker: the-smiths
entries.note: Same sentence as Bowie: liked together with Morrissey; borderline.

entries.speaker: the-smiths
entries.note: Praise for Raw Power; Marr tells his son to study it.

entries.speaker: pavement
entries.found: This album was a gateway towards sarcasm and questioning authority and the rightwing and Ronald Reagan – our Margaret Thatcher. I was listening to them in mid-late high school, 1981-82.
entries.citation: Stephen Malkmus, in the Observer's Soundtrack of My Life (2013): on the Dead Kennedys' Fresh Fruit for Rotting Vegetables, from his high-school years: "This album was a gateway towards sarcasm and questioning authority ... I was listening to them in mid-late high school, 1981-82."

entries.speaker: pavement
entries.found: Paul Westerberg wrote classic songs with a bit of cheek and hopelessness – and brilliance – combined. He's a poet: Let It Be was dramatic, romantic stuff.
entries.citation: Stephen Malkmus, in the Observer's Soundtrack of My Life (2013): choosing the Replacements' Let It Be as "the album that inspired my songwriting": "Paul Westerberg wrote classic songs with a bit of cheek and hopelessness – and brilliance – combined. He's a poet: Let It Be was dramatic, romantic stuff."

entries.speaker: pavement
entries.note: Only named alongside the Replacements as 80s college rock.

entries.speaker: pavement
entries.found: The 90s was when I became a hipster on a quest for unique stuff. Sister Ray is the ultimate song.
entries.citation: Stephen Malkmus, in the Observer's Soundtrack of My Life (2013): on the Velvet Underground: "The 90s was when I became a hipster on a quest for unique stuff. Sister Ray is the ultimate song."
entries.note: Borderline: "with me always", in the 90s (Pavement formed 1989); stated as a lasting favourite rather than a formative moment.

entries.speaker: pavement
entries.note: "Inspirational" in a general sense about a 1998 song, after Pavement formed.

entries.speaker: yeah-yeah-yeahs
entries.found: I can credit him for putting the idea in my head that I could sing too, as long as I sang my heart out.
entries.citation: Karen O, in the Observer's Soundtrack of My Life (2014): on Neutral Milk Hotel's On Avery Island, as "the record that inspired me to sing": "I can credit him for putting the idea in my head that I could sing too, as long as I sang my heart out."

entries.speaker: yeah-yeah-yeahs
entries.note: A pre-gig record she plays to get into a state; not about forming her music.

entries.speaker: yeah-yeah-yeahs
entries.note: Her friends listened to Fugazi before switching to the Dead; not her own account.

entries.speaker: sharon-van-etten
entries.found: My friend Paul played me this when I was in college, and it just killed me. It was so different, so minimal, and their voices together [Alan Sparhawk and Mimi Parker] were just beautiful.
entries.citation: Sharon Van Etten, in the Observer's Soundtrack of My Life (2015): on Low's Two-Step: "My friend Paul played me this when I was in college, and it just killed me. It was so different, so minimal, and their voices together ... were just beautiful."

entries.speaker: sharon-van-etten
entries.note: A song she plays before touring; fandom after her own music was under way.

entries.speaker: mac-demarco
entries.found: At high school, people generally liked the same music I did, but when I started getting into the Smiths everybody was like: “Dude, why are you listening to this crap?”
entries.citation: Mac DeMarco, in the Observer's Soundtrack of My Life (2015): on getting into the Smiths in high school: "when I started getting into the Smiths everybody was like: 'Dude, why are you listening to this crap?'"

entries.speaker: mac-demarco
entries.note: Song reminds him of moving to Vancouver; not said to shape his music.

entries.speaker: mac-demarco
entries.found: It was around the time I recorded 2 and I wanted to make my album sound exactly like this: really dry, really crisp 70s style.
entries.citation: Mac DeMarco, in the Observer's Soundtrack of My Life (2015): on Neil Young's Harvest, as "the record that influenced my breakthrough album": "It was around the time I recorded 2 and I wanted to make my album sound exactly like this: really dry, really crisp 70s style."

offMap.name: Fairport Convention
offMap.sentence: "I played British and Irish folk in an early band I had. We only performed one show and Rostam [Batmanglij, Vampire Weekend multi-instrumentalist] was also in the group, so this was the roots of Vampire Weekend. We covered 'Matty Groves' from this album."

offMap.name: DJ Shadow
offMap.sentence: "This was such a good introduction to sampling, and the idea that modern music could be made from the past. It inspired me in a big way."

offMap.name: Pearl Jam
offMap.sentence: "From the age of 10 to 13, the record that went everywhere with me ... was Pearl Jam's Ten"

offMap.name: Solex
offMap.sentence: "I got really into this Solex record called Pick Up ... this record just reaffirmed my place in the world to myself, 'Oh, I like weird music.'"

offMap.name: Public Enemy
offMap.sentence: "I loved hip-hop. ... the whole band agreed on Public Enemy. It just sounded completely new"

offMap.name: Cockney Rebel
offMap.sentence: "I heard it on a lads' holiday to Rhyl when I was 17 ... their first LP led me to Roxy, which led me into Bowie."

offMap.name: Roxy Music
offMap.sentence: "their first LP [1973's The Human Menagerie ] led me to Roxy, which led me into Bowie."

offMap.name: The Temptations (Carol Kaye's bass line)
offMap.sentence: "There was this woman bassist in the Motown house band called Carol Kaye. In this song, you hear her over the beginning, fantastic, a very musical bassline. I spent years trying to emulate it"

offMap.name: Kenny Rogers & The First Edition
offMap.sentence: "It's a great feeling to put on something you've had, and you've loved, since you were 13." (Ruby, Don't Take Your Love To Town; weak, fandom only)

offMap.name: Chic / Nile Rodgers
offMap.sentence: "My sister turned me on to Chic when their first album came out, in 1977, and I couldn't believe quite what I was hearing. ... He was a hero ... So he was someone I related to, and still do."

offMap.name: Hamilton Bohannon
offMap.sentence: "this scratchy guitar that you can hear influenced me and Nile Rodgers too."

offMap.name: Jimi Hendrix
offMap.sentence: "the gateway to me thinking the guitar was a cool thing was the E seventh chord. ... a slight change in E seventh that was in Purple Haze"

offMap.name: Miles Davis
offMap.sentence: "I picked up on Miles Davis, who was a huge influence on me."

offMap.name: Lonnie Donegan
offMap.sentence: "As soon as I heard skiffle, I loved it and I knew that I wanted to play it. I heard this track in 1954 and it was kind of key in my life."

offMap.name: Richard and Mimi Farina
offMap.sentence: "Richard and Mimi Fariña's Reflections in a Crystal Wind has been a big influence on me and I still listen to it now."

offMap.name: ESG
offMap.sentence: "I listened to it and I decided I wanted to be like those Scroggins sisters. ... Yeah Yeah Yeahs' first EP was largely Nick [Zinner] and I was trying to be like ESG but with guitar instead of bass."

offMap.name: Connie Francis / 50s-60s girl groups (solo work)
offMap.sentence: "nothing has greater influence than my dad's best of the 50s and 60s CD compilations. The doo-wop and girl group sound from those decades has shaped my melodic sensibility more than anything else." (about her solo work)

offMap.name: Leon Russell
offMap.sentence: "I realise there's a certain kind of vocalising I do that takes its cue from Leon Russell."

offMap.name: Elvis Costello
offMap.sentence: "Instead of studying I'd go in there and listen to Elvis Costello over and over until my ears hurt" (before starting the Pixies)

offMap.name: Jethro Tull
offMap.sentence: "I was heavily into Jethro Tull back then and I still am." (at 14)

offMap.name: Iggy Pop / XTC
offMap.sentence: "I would just sit in the dark and listen to Iggy Pop and XTC records for hours and hours." (before starting the Pixies; solo Iggy Pop is not on the map)

offMap.name: The Lemonheads
offMap.sentence: "Evan Dando's music was all about that for me. ... it's relatable, simple. I try to follow that."

offMap.name: Noveller
offMap.sentence: "I sit down with this track and just want to write, draw, sing, get out my guitar." (2015, current inspiration)

offMap.name: John Lennon / Plastic Ono Band
offMap.sentence: "I got the John Lennon/Plastic Ono Band album and I was like, whoa! ... aged 15 or 16 – I was starting to play in bands a bit ... I'm going to do this too."

offMap.name: Steely Dan
offMap.sentence: "Now that I think about it, my own music is pulled between both sides." (on Peg and dad rock)

offMap.name: Arthur Russell
offMap.sentence: "I love Arthur Russell. Wild Combination was the first track that made me pay attention to his music." (weak)
